title: Short Form Comedy
description: A fast-paced, writing-intensive dive into the world of sketch-writing, digital shorts, monologues, and stand-up comedy. We explore the foundational principals of scene-structure, joke-structure, and comedic voice through analysis of classic and contemporary examples, with an emphasis on developing your own unique point-of-view. Through in-class collaboration and a supportive “room-writing” environment, writers practice pitching, punching-up, producing, and performing individual, team, and group-generated material on a professional deadline, culminating in a performance/portfolio of written work, as well as tools to take a funny idea from concept to completion.

title: Storytelling for the Screen
description: Part one of a two-part program. Aimed at students who already have basic screenwriting strengths, and are in the intermediate-to-advanced skill range. While focus will depend on the writer-in-residence, the course will include sessions in plot and structure, character and dialogue, tension and conflict, tone and symbolism, and revision strategies.
prerequisites_raw: Consent of instructor, writing sample, upper-division standing.

title: Writing for Television
description: Introduction to fundamentals of writing for television including: the situation comedy, the hour-long drama, the MOW, the miniseries, and children's programming. Investigation of the practical and creative tools necessary for programming. Investigation of the practical and creative tools necessary for navigating successful television scripts.

title: The Writers Room
description: A writing-intensive practicum in creative collaboration. Working together, students will develop skills of improvisation, team-ideation, and room-writing to harness the power of diverse perspectives as we conceptualize, develop, and generate scripted material.

title: Workshop for the Screen
description: Part two of a two-part program. Team workshop structure will allow students to expand their screenwriting skills through a fundamental and intensive story-writing experience, an immersive and craft-focused writing calendar, with access to seasoned writers. Emphasis on multiple rounds of table-readings and group critiques.
prerequisites_raw: Consent of instructor, writing sample, upper-division standing.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory
description: Topics vary each year and may include such problems as the relation of film and other media to globalization, feminist aesthetics, critical race theories, technologies, algorithms, and the writings of key authors.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory
description: Topics vary each year and may include such problems as the relation of film and other media to structuralism, semiotics, metaphor/metonymy, point of view, and the writings of Burch, Barthes, Metz, Heath, Bordwell, Willemen, Wollen.
prerequisites_raw: Film Studies 146 and 192 and consent of instructor.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Algorithms and Culture
description: In this seminar, students take a critical design approach to analyze various algorithms (i.e., Search, PageRank), their relationship with their structured data (i.e., tweets), and their impact on contemporary infrastructures and social flows.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Contemporary Documentary
description: Documentaries are proliferating around the world, as are modes of documentary practice and studies. With screenings including theatrical, web-based, and interactive works from mainstream, alternative, and Indigenous perspectives, readings and discussion probe pressing issues of fact, fiction, and advocacy; and the media production of social spaces.

title: Cozy Games
description: Provides an opportunity to probe deeply into the genre of “cozy” games, which came to prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic with games like Animal Crossing: New Horizons (2020). We consider not only how gentle, wholesome, and domestic games predated the “cozy” label, but also how the moniker “cozy” predates cozy games (for instance, in cozy mysteries). In addition to questioning the typical gender coding of these games and their players, we will read and play extensively in order to think about the genre’s contested boundaries and why its classic themes of comfort, domesticity, and interpersonal relations often dovetail with (implied) violence, nature and the outdoors, and even death.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Disability and Media
description: This course introduces students to the central models within Disability Studies and their application to the field of Film and Media Studies, focusing especially on issues of representation, disability stardom, as well as media access.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: FemTech Lab
description: FemTech Lab is a theory/practice seminar on feminism, cyberfeminism, and feminist theories of technology. We engage the political potency of feminist media practicethe use of installations, performance, public engagements, and web-based platforms appealing for change or hacking systemic bias.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory Special Effects: Spectacular Technologies and the Body
description: This course focuses on special effects technologies in film, with an emphasis on their material natures and relationship(s) to the body including the bodies of viewers and of the many bodies involved in the effects production. Students learn theoretical tools from film and media theory, STS, and queer and environmental critique with which to engage with these biotechnical assemblages onscreen.

title: Topics in Contemporary Media Theory: Global News Media
description: Fake news, the corporate media, alternative facts. This class explores contemporary conversations about crises in news media forms by examining the histories, technologies, industries, policies, and cultural norms that shape global and local news cultures, specifically focusing on moving-image news and investigative content.
